specimens.name: Banquet
specimens.origin: Southeast Asia, by way of the Everglades
specimens.story: Banquet here got her name because that's what she treated the Everglades like — an all-you-can-eat buffet. Pythons like her have eaten so many marsh rabbits and raccoons that biologists literally can't find enough left to count. She can unhinge her jaw to swallow a deer whole, which is also how some of our regulars approach the smash burger. Raise a glass; she earned the wall.

specimens.name: Vlad
specimens.story: Vlad is gorgeous, venomous, and has absolutely no natural predators in the Atlantic — a combination that also describes a few people at last call. One lionfish can wipe out most of the young fish on a reef patch in weeks. The good news: they're delicious. Eating invasives is conservation, which makes your fish sandwich basically volunteer work.

specimens.name: Iggy
specimens.origin: Central & South America, via the pet trade
specimens.story: Iggy spent his years eating South Florida's landscaping and digging burrows that collapse seawalls. When it gets below 40°F, iguanas like him famously go rigid and drop straight out of trees — the only weather forecast Florida ever needed. He fell for the last time in the iguana blizzard of '22, and now he supervises the taproom.

specimens.name: Chompsky
specimens.origin: Brought by Spanish explorers in the 1500s
specimens.story: Chompsky descends from hogs Hernando de Soto dropped off in Florida five hundred years ago, making him more of a local than anyone drinking here tonight. Wild hogs plow up wetlands like rototillers and eat literally anything, causing billions in damage a year. He lost an argument with a hunter in Okeechobee and won a permanent bar tab here.

specimens.name: Duke
specimens.origin: South America, imported to eat sugarcane beetles in 1936
specimens.story: Duke was brought in to protect Florida's sugarcane. He did not protect the sugarcane. Instead, cane toads spread everywhere, ooze a toxin strong enough to take down a curious dog, and grow to the size of a dinner plate. A cautionary tale about hiring the wrong contractor — he sits here as a warning to us all.

specimens.name: Flash
specimens.origin: Amazon Basin — one of the only invasives Florida invited on purpose
specimens.story: Flash is the rare invader with a work visa: Florida stocked peacock bass in the '80s specifically to eat other invasive fish, and it mostly worked. He spent a decade terrorizing the canals of Miami-Dade before an angler with a topwater lure ended his run. He's the only one on this wall who was doing his job when he went.
